title: Nothing Can Separate
subtitle: Romans in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Paul wrote to believers in Rome he had never met, and handed them the whole gospel in a single letter: a world that shows its Maker in every leaf, a line of lamps all burned low, a pardon given freely, an old man counting stars, a river where the old life is buried and a new one climbs out. Then a man honest enough to say he does what he hates, a child calling Abba, a creation groaning like a woman in labor, a wild olive branch grafted into an old root, and a long list of friends greeted by name.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts: the gospel that is not ashamed, peace with God, life in the Spirit, the mercy that reaches everyone, and love worked out at the table. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the letter touches—a broken seal, a seed, a clay jar, an olive branch, a table with room at it—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open Paul's letter to the Romans alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.lightHint: Near 'beloved in Rome' (Romans 1:7–12) in Part 1: Not Ashamed

parts.lightHint: Near 'where we stand' (Romans 5:1–2) in Part 2: Peace with God

parts.lightHint: Near 'great sorrow' (Romans 9:1–5) in Part 4: Grafted In

paintings.title: beloved in Rome
paintings.epigraph: “to all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints”
paintings.poem:
he had never seen their faces.
never broken bread
at their tables.

still, the first thing he tells them
is who they are:
beloved.
called.

and the second thing:
I long to see you,
so that we can
lift each other up.

it is a strange letter
that begins by saying
I need you too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “beloved in Rome” (Romans 1:7–12) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: not ashamed
paintings.epigraph: “For I am not ashamed of the Good News of Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes”
paintings.poem:
Rome had its marble,
its roads that ran
to the edge of the world,
its gods on every corner.

and Paul was coming
with a story about
a crucified carpenter.

he wasn't embarrassed.

not because the story
was impressive,
but because it worked:

it had already
turned him around
on a road
just like this one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not ashamed” (Romans 1:16)—where the poem notes, “on a road just like this one”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the things that are made
paintings.epigraph: “For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made”
paintings.poem:
before there was a scroll,
there was the sky.

before a single prophet spoke,
the fig tree was already
putting out its leaves
on time.

the mountains don't say
the Maker's name.

they just stand there
being far too large
and far too careful
to have made themselves.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the things that are made” (Romans 1:20)—where the poem notes, “and far too careful to have made themselves”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: kindness
paintings.epigraph: “the goodness of God leads you to repentance”
paintings.poem:
you would think
it takes a threat
to turn someone around.

a shout.
a locked gate.
a fist.

but here it says
it was kindness:

patience that waited
longer than it had to,
a light left on,
a door that stayed open.

most of us came home
because someone
was that good to us
first.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Romans 2:4 (“was that good to us first”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: all
paintings.epigraph: “For there is no distinction, for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God”
paintings.poem:
the teacher and the thief.
the priest and the one
who never goes near the temple.

line up every lamp
in the city
and not one of them
is burning as bright
as it was made to.

it isn't a verdict
meant to crush you.

it's the ground,
level,
so that when grace comes
nobody has to climb
to reach it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “all” (Romans 3:22–23)—where the poem notes, “nobody has to climb to reach it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: freely
paintings.epigraph: “being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus”
paintings.poem:
a pardon
is a strange kind of paper.

it doesn't say
you were innocent.

it doesn't say
you earned your way out.

it says:
you are free to go.
the debt is answered.
someone paid.

freely,
the word says,
the way the sun
falls on a field
that never
asked for it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “freely” (Romans 3:24)—where the poem notes, “that never asked for it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: counted
paintings.epigraph: “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”
paintings.poem:
he hadn't built a temple yet.
hadn't kept a single law
that Moses would later carry
down the mountain.

he only stood outside his tent
and looked up
and believed
the One who told him
to count.

and God wrote it down
in the column
marked righteous.

that is the whole
of what he brought:
a yes
under the stars.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “counted” (Romans 4:3)—where the poem notes, “a yes under the stars”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the things that are not
paintings.epigraph: “calls the things that are not, as though they were.”
paintings.poem:
about a hundred years old,
the letter says,
and Sarah long past
the age for children.

he didn't pretend
his body was young.
he looked straight at it.

and then he looked
at the promise,
and the promise was bigger.

God calls the things that are not
as though they were,

the way a farmer
talks about a harvest
while holding
a single seed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the things that are not” (Romans 4:17–21)—where the poem notes, “while holding a single seed”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: where we stand
paintings.epigraph: “through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand.”
paintings.poem:
not a truce.
not a ceasefire
with both sides
still watching.

peace.

and a door
that doesn't close
behind you.

you don't have to
earn your way back in
each morning.

this is the grace
you stand in,
like standing
in the sun.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “where we stand” (Romans 5:1–2)—where the poem notes, “like standing in the sun”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: hope does not disappoint
paintings.epigraph: “hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.”
paintings.poem:
suffering, then
staying,
then a character
that has been tested,
then hope.

it's a long road
and nobody would choose it.

but the hope at the end
is not the kind
that leaves you
standing at the gate
at nightfall
with no one coming.

it holds,
because the love
was already
poured in.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5:3–5)—where the poem notes, “was already poured in”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: while we were yet sinners
paintings.epigraph: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
paintings.poem:
not after we cleaned up.
not once we said sorry
and meant it.

while.

while the door was shut
from our side.
while we were
still walking the other way.

someone might die
for a good man,
Paul says.
maybe.

but this love
went first,
and didn't wait
to see
if we'd be worth it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Romans 5:6–8 (“to see if we'd be worth it”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: much more
paintings.epigraph: “where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly”
paintings.poem:
the stones were real.
dark, and many,
and piled up high.

but the tide
didn't argue with them.

it just kept coming,
wave on quiet wave,

until you could not find
where they had been.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “much more” (Romans 5:20–21)—where the poem notes, “until you could not find where they had been”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: buried and raised
paintings.epigraph: “so we also might walk in newness of life.”
paintings.poem:
down into the water,
like being laid
in the ground.

the old life
doesn't come back up.

that is the point.

what comes up
is dripping and new
and not quite sure
how to walk yet,

and the first step
on the bank
is the first step
of a different life.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “buried and raised” (Romans 6:3–4)—where the poem notes, “is the first step of a different life”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the open lock
paintings.epigraph: “Being made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness.”
paintings.poem:
the chain is still lying there.
you could put it back on.

some mornings
the old master calls
and your feet remember
the way.

but the lock is open.

you belong
to someone else now,

and he doesn't
keep chains.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the open lock” (Romans 6:17–18)—where the poem notes, “and he doesn't keep chains”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: wages and gift
paintings.epigraph: “For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
paintings.poem:
wages are what you earn.
you work, and at sundown
they count it into your hand,
exactly.

a gift
you can't earn.
you can only
open your hand.

one side of the sentence
is a payment.
the other
is a present.

and the second half
is the one
God wants to give.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “wages and gift” (Romans 6:23)—where the poem notes, “is the one God wants to give”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: what I hate
paintings.epigraph: “For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.”
paintings.poem:
he doesn't hide it.
the great apostle
writes it down
for a church he's never met:

I want to do good
and I don't.
I don't want to do wrong
and I do.

smooth the wax,
write it again,
watch it go crooked
in the same place.

if you have ever
made the same promise
to yourself
for the hundredth time,

you are not alone
in this chapter.40
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “what I hate” (Romans 7:15–19)—where the poem notes, “you are not alone in this chapter.40”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: who will deliver me
paintings.epigraph: “Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!”
paintings.poem:
not what.
who.

he doesn't ask
for a better method,
a stricter rule,
one more try.

he asks for a person.

and before the question
has finished echoing,
he's already saying
thank you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “who will deliver me” (Romans 7:24–25)—where the poem notes, “he's already saying thank you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: now
paintings.epigraph: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus”
paintings.poem:
there is therefore now

not someday,
after you've improved.

not on good days only.

now.

the seat is empty.
nobody is reading out
the list.

you can walk
across the square
in the morning light
and no one
will stop you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “now” (Romans 8:1)—where the poem notes, “and no one will stop you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: Abba
paintings.epigraph: “you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!””
paintings.poem:
a servant says
master
and keeps his eyes down.

a child
runs in without knocking
and says
Abba.

you weren't hired.
you were adopted.

the Spirit inside you
is the one
who taught your mouth
the word.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “Abba” (Romans 8:15–16), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: labor
paintings.epigraph: “For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now.”
paintings.poem:
the field is aching.
the hills are waiting.
even the frost
seems to be holding its breath.

the whole world
is groaning,

but not the way
a dying thing groans.

the way a mother does
when something new
is almost here.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Romans 8:19–22 (“when something new is almost here”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: too deep for words
paintings.epigraph: “the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.”
paintings.poem:
some nights
you don't have the words.

you kneel down
and all that comes out
is a sigh.

it is enough.

someone else
is praying underneath
your prayer,

and he knows
exactly what you meant.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “too deep for words” (Romans 8:26–27)—where the poem notes, “and he knows exactly what you meant”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: together for good
paintings.epigraph: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God”
paintings.poem:
salt alone
is bitter in the mouth.
leaven alone
is sour.
flour alone is dust,
and fire burns.

it doesn't say
all things are good.

it says
they are being worked
together,

by hands
that know how to make
bread.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “together for good” (Romans 8:28)—where the poem notes, “that know how to make bread”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: for us
paintings.epigraph: “If God is for us, who can be against us?”
paintings.poem:
who is going to accuse you?
the One who justifies?

who is going to condemn you?
the One who died for you,
and rose,
and is praying for you
right now?

the case has no one
left to bring it.

God is not
across the room from you.

he is standing
at the gate.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “for us” (Romans 8:31–34)—where the poem notes, “he is standing at the gate”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: more than conquerors
paintings.epigraph: “in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.”
paintings.poem:
not around
these things.
not above them.

in them.

the hunger is real.
the storm is real.
the danger does not
politely step aside.

and still the boat
comes through,

not because
the sea was easy,

but because of the one
who loves the people
in the boat.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “more than conquerors” (Romans 8:35–37)—where the poem notes, “who loves the people in the boat”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: nothing
paintings.epigraph: “nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
paintings.poem:
not death.
not life.
not angels,
not rulers,
not today,
not whatever tomorrow brings.

not the height
of the sky
or the depth
of the sea.

Paul goes looking
through all of creation
for one thing
strong enough.

he comes back
empty-handed

and glad.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “nothing” (Romans 8:38–39)—where the poem notes, “and glad”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: great sorrow
paintings.epigraph: “I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart.”
paintings.poem:
here, in the middle
of the most joyful letter
he ever wrote,
he stops.

his own people.
his own family.
the ones who were given
the covenants,
the promises,
the fathers.

he doesn't argue here.
he grieves.

and you can tell
from the grief
how much
he loves them.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “great sorrow” (Romans 9:1–5)—where the poem notes, “how much he loves them”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: vessels of mercy
paintings.epigraph: “the riches of his glory on vessels of mercy”
paintings.poem:
the clay can ask
why.

and the potter
is patient with it,
more patient
than the clay
can understand.

there are things here
too deep for us.

but see what he is making:
not trophies,
not tools,

vessels of mercy,
so there is something
to carry
the riches of his glory

to everyone.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “vessels of mercy” (Romans 9:20–23) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: near
paintings.epigraph: “The word is near you, in your mouth, and in your heart”
paintings.poem:
you don't have to climb
into heaven
to bring him down.

you don't have to dig
into the deep
to bring him up.

he already came down.
he already rose.

the word is near you,
as near as your own breath,

and whoever calls,
Jew or Greek,
anyone,
will be saved.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “near” (Romans 10:8–13)—where the poem notes, “anyone, will be saved”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: beautiful feet
paintings.epigraph: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace”
paintings.poem:
nobody writes poems
about feet.

cracked heels.
dust between the toes.
the long road
still on them.

but someone had to walk
to where you were.

someone had to open
their mouth
and say it,

and every mile
of that road
is beautiful.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “beautiful feet” (Romans 10:14–15)—where the poem notes, “of that road is beautiful”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the olive tree
paintings.epigraph: “it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you.”
paintings.poem:
a wild branch,
cut from a hillside
where no one tended it,

bound into an old tree
with deep roots
and a long memory.

don't boast, Paul says.
you didn't plant the root.
the root is holding you.

and God is able
to graft the old branches
back in again.

his gifts
don't get taken back.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the olive tree” (Romans 11:17–24)—where the poem notes, “his gifts don't get taken back”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the depth
paintings.epigraph: “Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God!”
paintings.poem:
three chapters
of hard questions,

and at the bottom of them
he doesn't find
a neat answer.

he finds a well
so deep
he can't see the end of it.

so he stops arguing
and starts to sing:
from him, through him,
to him, all things.

sometimes worship
is what you do
at the bottom
of your questions.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the depth” (Romans 11:33–36)—where the poem notes, “at the bottom of your questions”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: living sacrifice
paintings.epigraph: “be transformed by the renewing of your mind”
paintings.poem:
not a lamb this time.
not a bull,
not a bag of grain.

you.

and not dead on the altar,
but alive,
getting up in the morning,
going to work,
setting the table.

the world will press you
into its shape
if you let it.

let God
change the mind first.

the rest of you
will follow.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1–2)—where the poem notes, “the rest of you will follow”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: without pretending
paintings.epigraph: “Let love be without hypocrisy.”
paintings.poem:
the same love
at the table
as in the street.

the same kindness
when no one
is watching.

nothing painted on.
no face put on
for company.

just a plain cup,
full,

and all the way through
the same clay.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “without pretending” (Romans 12:9–10)—where the poem notes, “and all the way through the same clay”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: with
paintings.epigraph: “Rejoice with those who rejoice. W eep with those who weep.”
paintings.poem:
some days, the wine.
some days, the water.

the gift is not
to have the answer.

it's to be
at the table.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “with” (Romans 12:15)—where the poem notes, “it's to be at the table”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: overcome
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”
paintings.poem:
he wronged you.
you remember
every word.

and here is the strange
instruction:

if he's hungry,
feed him.
if he's thirsty,
bring him water.

leave the settling of scores
to God.

evil wants
to make you
into its own shape.

bread on the doorstep
is how you
refuse.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of Romans 12:17–21?

paintings.title: the night is far gone
paintings.epigraph: “The night is far gone, and the day is near.”
paintings.poem:
you can feel it
before you see it:

the dark getting thinner,
a rooster somewhere,
the air changing.

wake up.

take off
what belonged to the night.

put on the light
like a clean garment,

and walk
the way people walk
when the day
has already come.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the night is far gone” (Romans 13:11–12)—where the poem notes, “when the day has already come”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: welcome
paintings.epigraph: “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.”
paintings.poem:
one eats meat.
one eats only vegetables.
one keeps the holy days.
one keeps them all alike.

they could argue
till the lamps went out.

or they could remember
how they got a seat
at this table
in the first place:

someone made room
for them
before they had
anything right.

pull out a stool.
make room.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “welcome” (Romans 15:7)—where the poem notes, “pull out a stool. make room”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the Lord's
paintings.epigraph: “If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.”
paintings.poem:
none of us
lives to himself.

none of us dies
to himself either.

on this side
or the other,
waking or sleeping,

the vineyard
still has
the same owner.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the Lord's” (Romans 14:7–8)—where the poem notes, “still has the same owner”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the God of hope
paintings.epigraph: “Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope”
paintings.poem:
he doesn't pray
that they'll try harder
at hoping.

he prays
that God will fill them,

like a jar
set under the spring,

until the joy
runs over the rim

and the ground around it
gets wet too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the God of hope” (Romans 15:13)—where the poem notes, “and the ground around it gets wet too”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: greet them all
paintings.epigraph: “I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae”
paintings.poem:
after all the great chapters,
he ends with names.

Phoebe, who helped so many.
Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks,
and the church in their house.
Mary, who worked hard.
Andronicus and Junia,
in Christ before he was.
Persis, the beloved.
Rufus, and his mother,
a mother to Paul too.

and Tertius, holding the pen,
slips in his own hello.

the gospel, it turns out,
has a lot of friends.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “greet them all” (Romans 16:1–16)—where the poem notes, “the gospel, it turns out, has a lot of friends”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?
